summary: Adjudicate whether distribution-aligned judges (Chen 2025 / Li 2025) learn item-level disagreement or only global smoothing, by re-training the objective on a real 6-rater SE panel and scoring it against matched held-out raters with explicit item-independent smoothing and placebo controls.
hypothesis: Mechanism: a KL-to-pooled-pmf objective can lower KL via two routes: (a) global calibration, i.e. softening a median-tracking predictor toward the marginal rating spread, or (b) item-specific dispersion, i.e. predicting WHICH items split raters. Circular evaluation on the same pooled distribution (Chen/Li) cannot separate them; our F2 and Artificial Hivemind predict route (a) dominates. Expected direction: >=70% of the held-out-rater NLL gain of KL training over point SFT is reproduced by point SFT plus one global temperature and one marginal-mixture weight; the residual item-specific share concentrates in the Partial stratum; on the Low stratum neither judge beats the matched held-out human (HCA <= 1). If instead the item-specific share is large and Low-stratum HCA rises, the Chen/Li claim survives a fair test.
mve: Benchmark: commit messages (Zeng et al., 800 msgs x 6 raters, What/Why, developer+generated pools), 5-fold item CV. Base: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, LoRA r=16, score read from the 0-4 score-token logits (token ids already known from the smoke test). Objectives: (O1) point SFT to pooled median; (O2) KL to the empirical 6-rater pmf (Chen-style, no adversarial term); (O3) O1 + post-hoc global temperature tau and marginal-mixture lambda fitted on train folds = strongest item-independent smoother; (O4) KL to dispersion-permuted targets (same median, another item's spread) = placebo. Metrics: leave-one-rater-out NLL and CRPS per stratum (each of the 6 raters scored individually on test items), Spearman(predicted entropy, human std), entropy->Low-stratum AUROC, stratified HCA and Delta_match vs matched human, and the 'smoothing share' = (NLL_O1 - NLL_O3)/(NLL_O1 - NLL_O2). GPU-hours: 4 objectives x 5 folds x ~12 min ~= 4 GPU-h training + ~1 GPU-h eval; pilot = What criterion, 1 fold, O1/O2/O3 ~= 1 GPU-h.
contribution_type: empirical finding + diagnostic (smoothing-share decomposition; fair-test protocol for trained distributional judges)
prior_work: 2505.12301 (Chen, Distributional LLM-as-a-Judge): same KL objective but train and test on the same pooled distribution; delta = held-out-rater + consensus strata + explicit temperature/marginal smoother and dispersion-permuted placebo on an SE panel. ; 2510.00263 (Li, Judging with Confidence): population distribution from synthetic personas, pairwise; delta = real ordinal raters, Likert, smoothing-share decomposition. ; 2510.22954 (Artificial Hivemind): diagnostic on untrained judges/RMs with 25 ratings per item; delta = trained judges on a 6-rater panel scored against a matched human. ; 2410.14632 (Zhang, Diverging Preferences): Diverging-ID AUROC for scalar RMs; delta = generative judge, temperature control isolates smoothing, matched human reference. ; 2210.16133 (Baan, Stop Measuring Calibration When Humans Disagree): instance-level calibration metrics; delta = applied to a trained judge under leave-one-rater-out scoring. ; 2503.03064 (Wang/Zhang/Choi): inference-only judgment distributions; delta = trained distributions with a smoothing null.
so_what: Either outcome matters: if smoothing dominates, the NeurIPS-2025 distributional-judge gain is an evaluation artifact of the same family as the alignment mirage and distributional judges must be validated on held-out raters; if item-specific dispersion is learned, it is the first SE judge with validated disagreement-awareness on contested items.

summary: Resolve Ni 2025 (RLVR-style reasoning hurts disagreement modelling) against RM-R1/J1/JudgeLRM (RL judges beat SFT) with a 2x2 GRPO design, {CoT on/off} x {hard median-match reward / proper-scoring reward on the rater pmf}, evaluated by consensus stratum against a matched human on SE Likert data.
hypothesis: Mechanism: the two lines aggregate over different item mixes and conflate two factors. A hard verifiable reward (match the pooled label) is maximised by a point mass at the median, so RL sharpens the score distribution and collapses predicted dispersion (Ni's degradation) while raising High-consensus accuracy (the RM-R1/J1 gain); the reasoning trace itself is not the cause. Expected: hard-reward GRPO improves High-stratum alpha/HCA over SFT but REDUCES Low-stratum held-out-rater NLL and entropy->Low AUROC; proper-scoring (log-score or CRPS) reward GRPO keeps the High gain and preserves or improves Low-stratum NLL, with CoT on/off a second-order effect. If no-CoT hard-reward also degrades Low NLL, the reward is the culprit; if CoT degrades regardless of reward, Ni's account holds at training time.
mve: Benchmark: commit messages, 640 train / 160 test, both pools, 3 seeds on the decisive cells. Base: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct LoRA; trl 1.6 GRPO with vLLM rollouts on a separate GPU (4 rollouts per prompt, <=256 output tokens no-CoT / <=640 CoT). Output: optional <think> block then a verbalised pmf over 0-4 (for no-CoT the pmf is read from score-token logits). Rewards: R_hard = 1[argmax == pooled median] (+format); R_proper = mean over the 6 raters of log q(r_i), or -CRPS(q, empirical pmf). Baselines: point SFT and KL-SFT (from idea 1), plus the released QwQ-32B and frontier outputs already on disk. Metrics: per-stratum alpha vs pooled and Delta_match vs matched human, HCA per stratum, held-out-rater NLL, entropy->Low AUROC, hedging/sharpness check (Tan 2026 confidence-reward hacking), CoT length vs stratum. GPU-hours: 4 cells x ~2.5 h + 2 extra seeds on 2 cells ~= 15 GPU-h; pilot = no-CoT x {hard, proper}, 1 seed, What only ~= 3-4 GPU-h. Fallback: a 3B Coder model if 7B GRPO exceeds the ~22 GB free per card.
contribution_type: empirical finding + new method (first RL judge trained with a proper-scoring reward over a real annotator distribution)
prior_work: 2506.19467 (Ni, Can Reasoning Help Disagreement): off-the-shelf reasoning models on NLP classification; delta = controlled training with a reward x reasoning factorial on Likert SE data, matched-human strata. ; 2505.10320 (J1) / 2505.02387 (RM-R1) / 2504.00050 (JudgeLRM): binary verifiable rewards, pooled evaluation; delta = distribution-matching reward and consensus-stratified evaluation against a held-out human. ; 2510.00263 (Li): GRPO with Brier on binary pairwise labels from synthetic personas; delta = ordinal pmf of real raters, CoT factor, strata. ; 2603.17145 (REAL): regression-aware RL to a single gold score; delta = distributional target over raters. ; 2605.20740 (Park, Distribution-Aware Reward): CRPS reward for LLM regression; delta = judge setting with an empirical annotator pmf. ; 2607.04332 (Tan) / 2507.16806 (RLCR): calibrate P(my answer is correct); delta = reward targets P(another rater says k), hedging audited.
so_what: Settles whether reasoning judges are structurally unfit for contested items or merely mis-rewarded; a positive proper-scoring result gives SE a recipe for RL judges that stop collapsing disagreement, a negative one corroborates Ni at training time and extends it to Likert quality judging.

summary: Adjudicate Orlikowski 2025 (per-annotator fine-tuning memorises) against jury learning / PAL / VPL (learnable rater structure) by testing whether SE rater heterogeneity is leniency (a two-parameter per-rater affine shift) or taste (rater x item interaction), across seen-rater, k-shot new-rater and zero-shot new-rater regimes on the 6- and 9-rater panels.
hypothesis: Mechanism: in small expert panels rating SE artifacts, much inter-rater variance is scale use (strict vs lenient raters, floor effects on Why) rather than content-dependent preference; an annotator-ID-conditioned LoRA can only add value beyond a per-rater affine recalibration if the rater x item interaction is both large and reproducible. Expected: a two-way decomposition of the 800 x 6 matrix shows rater main effects much larger than reproducible interaction; per-rater affine recalibration of a pooled-distribution judge captures most of the seen-rater gain of full ID-conditioning; ID-conditioning wins only on Low-stratum items and does not transfer zero-shot to an unseen rater (Orlikowski), but k = 20-50 calibration items recover it (PAL/VPL). The 9-rater readability panel is expected to show a larger interaction share, i.e. genuine taste.
mve: Primary: commit messages (6 raters, leave-one-rater-out folds); secondary: readability (9 raters x 200 snippets, 5-fold over items). Step 0 (CPU): two-way random-effects decomposition and split-half reliability of the rater x item interaction. Base: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B LoRA. Conditions: (A) pooled-pmf judge (KL to the 5 training raters); (B) annotator-ID-conditioned judge trained on the 5 raters' individual labels with a 'Rater r' prefix; (C) A + per-rater affine (a_r, b_r) fitted on the held-out rater's k calibration items (PEBS-style control); (D) B + new-rater embedding fitted on the same k items (VPL/PAL-style). Metrics: held-out-rater NLL/MAE per stratum for seen raters on held-out items and for the unseen rater at k in {0, 20, 50, 100}; Delta_match and HCA of the conditioned prediction against that rater; share of gain attributable to affine vs interaction. GPU-hours: CM 6 folds x 2 trained conditions x ~12 min ~= 2.5 GPU-h; RD 5 folds x 2 x ~5 min ~= 1 GPU-h; pilot = 1 CM fold ~= 0.5-1 GPU-h.
contribution_type: empirical finding + diagnostic (leniency-vs-taste decomposition for small panels)
prior_work: 2502.20897 (Orlikowski, Beyond Demographics): per-annotator fine-tunes memorise on NLP subjective text; delta = SE Likert, explicit affine control, k-shot new-rater regime. ; 2202.02950 (Jury Learning): per-annotator models for seen annotators only; delta = unseen-rater test and reproducibility of interaction. ; 2406.08469 (PAL) / 2408.10075 (VPL): latent user embeddings on pairwise chat preferences; delta = Likert SE, affine baseline, matched-human evaluation. ; 2606.27578 (PEBS): post-hoc per-rater affine calibration of an RM; delta = head-to-head vs learned conditioning in a generative judge, unseen-rater transfer, strata. ; 2604.08425 (DiADEM): predicts who disagrees from demographics; delta = no demographics, SE artifacts. ; 2605.11865 (variance-aware RM): identifiability of per-item variance flagged open; delta = empirical interaction reliability on 3/6/9-rater panels.
so_what: Tells SE benchmark builders whether to collect rater IDs and calibration items (taste) or simply recalibrate scales (leniency), and resolves the perspectivist contradiction on the panel sizes SE actually has rather than on dense crowds.

summary: Test whether the low effective vote count of judge panels (Nine Judges) and the null result for multi-agent SE judges (our F4) come from a shared pooled training target, by training rater-specialist judge panels and measuring effective independent votes and contested-item value against a matched human.
hypothesis: Mechanism: judges that all fit the same pooled label converge on the same median predictor, so ensembling seeds, prompts or agents adds little independent information (n_eff ~= 1-2) and their spread cannot proxy human disagreement; judges trained on different individual raters inherit rater-level variance and yield a higher n_eff whose spread tracks human dispersion. Expected: seed- and bootstrap-ensembles of pooled LoRAs have n_eff < 2 and spread->Low AUROC near chance (explaining F4 and Nine Judges); rater-specialist panels reach n_eff ~= 3-4 on the 6-rater panel with AUROC clearly above chance, while their panel median matches but does not exceed the pooled judge on High items.
mve: Benchmark: commit messages, 640/160 split. Base: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B LoRA. Panels of six: (P1) 6 rater-specialist LoRAs, each trained on one rater's What/Why labels; (P2) 6 pooled-median LoRAs with different seeds; (P3) 6 bootstrap-resampled pooled LoRAs; (P4) existing SE-Jury / CodeVisionary and frontier 3-run outputs from disk (free). Metrics: design-effect n_eff = m / (1 + (m-1) rho_bar) from inter-judge ordinal alpha/correlation, panel spread -> Low-stratum AUROC and Spearman with human std, panel-median HCA and Delta_match per stratum, specialist-vs-own-rater alpha (are specialists actually distinct?). GPU-hours: 18 LoRA runs x ~10 min ~= 3 GPU-h; pilot = 3 specialists + 3 seeds ~= 1 GPU-h.
contribution_type: empirical finding (source of panel diversity) + diagnostic (n_eff for judge panels)

summary: Adjudicate noise-robust preference optimisation (rDPO/ROPO/Dr.DPO: disagreement = flip noise) against pluralistic reward modelling (disagreement = signal) on real 6-rater commit-message pairs, measuring the trained policy's implicit preference separately on contested vs uncontested held-out pairs.
hypothesis: Mechanism: noise-robust PO assumes a scalar, item-independent flip rate; if real SE disagreement is heteroskedastic and item-specific, a one-coin noise model fits the 6 x 400 pair matrix worse than an item-level dispersion model, and DPO variants that down-weight or flip-correct contested pairs train policies that are over-decisive exactly on contested held-out pairs, while soft-label (preference-rate) DPO stays calibrated there at no cost on uncontested pairs. Expected: the item-level model wins the Step-0 likelihood; rDPO/cDPO ~= standard DPO on uncontested accuracy but worse Brier vs empirical rate on contested pairs than GAPO-style soft DPO; dropping contested pairs leaves uncontested accuracy unchanged (they carry no removable 'noise').
mve: Data: 400 pairs (developer vs generated message per diff) with 6 per-rater preferences from What+Why sums; contested = preference rate in [2/6, 4/6]. Step 0 (CPU): one-coin flip model vs per-item Beta dispersion model, leave-one-rater-out likelihood. Step 1: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B LoRA policy generating commit messages from diffs; 320/80 pair split, 3 seeds; variants: standard DPO (majority label), cDPO/rDPO with epsilon = empirical disagreement rate, GAPO soft-label DPO with target = rate, contested-dropped DPO. Metrics on held-out pairs: implicit-reward accuracy on uncontested pairs, Brier/ECE of sigma(beta * log-ratio) vs empirical rate on contested pairs, decisiveness |p_hat - 0.5| by stratum. Secondary: best-of-8 generations on 40 held-out diffs scored by the pooled and distributional judges from idea 1 and by two frontier judges, reported by stratum of the source diff. GPU-hours: 4 variants x 3 seeds x ~12 min ~= 2.5 GPU-h + ~1 GPU-h BoN sampling; pilot = DPO vs soft DPO, 1 seed ~= 1 GPU-h.
contribution_type: empirical finding (downstream) + diagnostic (noise-model vs dispersion-model test for small panels)
prior_work: 2403.00409 (rDPO) / 2404.04102 (ROPO) / 2407.07880 (Dr.DPO): robustness to synthetic label flips; delta = real multi-rater disagreement, contested-vs-uncontested split of the policy's behaviour. ; 2409.06691 (GAPO): soft labels from AI simulation; delta = real rater preference rates on SE generation. ; 2608.12330 (RA-DPO): agreement-weighted DPO on classification; delta = generation task, policy calibration on contested pairs. ; 2410.14632 (Zhang): RM decisiveness on divisive pairs; delta = the DPO policy itself, downstream, SE. ; 2405.16455 (Xiao) / 2511.08594 (Soft Preference Learning) / 2608.10126 (PA-RLHF): majority-collapse theory and synthetic groups; delta = measured on real SE pairs by stratum. ; 2403.09032 (CodeUltraFeedback): DPO on GPT-3.5-judged code preferences; delta = human multi-rater preferences. ; 2507.10906 (Zeng): benchmark source, ratings averaged; delta = used disaggregated as preference rates. ; 2510.01458 (Im): generalisation theory under noisy feedback; delta = empirical test of the scalar-noise assumption.
so_what: Decides whether SE preference data with disagreement should be cleaned (noise view) or modelled (signal view) before DPO, and gives the first real-data measurement of the predicted majority collapse on contested items.

summary: Resolve 'readability is unresolvable' (our HCA discriminative power S = 0.14) against published readability-judge alignment by testing whether per-rater readability ratings are individually predictable (stable taste) or unpredictable beyond the marginal (noise), using pooled, annotator-conditioned and rater-specialist judges on the 9-rater CoReEval panel.
hypothesis: Mechanism: a low S can arise from (a) genuine pluralism, i.e. stable rater-specific criteria that a pooled target averages away but per-rater models can learn, or (b) measurement noise, i.e. ratings unpredictable from the snippet by any model. Published alignment numbers correlate with the pooled mean and cannot distinguish these. Expected: split-half reliability of rater x item effects is moderate and rater-specialist judges beat the pooled judge on per-rater held-out MAE for a subset of raters (pluralism for some raters, noise for others); a surface-feature regression (length, nesting depth, identifier length) reproduces most of the published pooled correlation, showing the reported 'alignment' was with marginal snippet features.
mve: Benchmark: readability (Scalabrino, 200 snippets x 9 raters, 1-5), 5-fold over snippets. Base: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B. Two fits because n is tiny: (i) light, frozen judge score-token logits + hidden-state linear probes per rater; (ii) LoRA with rater-ID conditioning vs pooled-mean LoRA vs 9 specialist LoRAs (short runs). Baselines: marginal per-rater predictor, surface-feature ridge regression, frontier judge outputs already on disk. Metrics: per-rater held-out MAE/NLL vs marginal, split-half reliability of the interaction, HCA and Delta_match vs each held-out rater by stratum, share of the pooled-mean correlation explained by the surface model. GPU-hours: probes ~= 0.3 GPU-h; LoRA 5 folds x 11 runs x ~3 min ~= 3 GPU-h; pilot = probes only ~= 0.5 GPU-h.
contribution_type: empirical finding + diagnostic (per-rater predictability as a benchmark-level readability test)
prior_work: 2605.25296 (Mokhova, Subjective Code Preferences): LLM Likert distributions polarised vs 73 engineers; delta = trained per-rater models and a predictability test on the 9-rater panel. ; 2502.20897 (Orlikowski): memorisation of annotators; delta = memorisation vs taste separated by split-half reliability of the interaction. ; 2512.22245 (linear probes for judge calibration): cheap confidence heads; delta = per-rater heads as a pluralism probe. ; 2503.05965 (Guerdan, Rating Indeterminacy): validation framework for multi-valid ratings; delta = trained-judge operationalisation on SE readability. ; 2510.22954 (Artificial Hivemind): judges fail where raters diverge; delta = small panel, per-rater learnability rather than dense-crowd diagnostics. ; 2507.16587 (Crupi): SE judge validation on pooled labels; delta = per-rater evaluation.
so_what: If readability is pluralistic, readability judges should be rater-conditioned and benchmarks should stop reporting pooled correlations; if it is noise, the benchmark needs replacing before any judge claim is meaningful. Either way it explains the conflict between our S and the literature's alignment numbers.

summary: Gain decomposition of pooled-label SFT: measure whether the agreement gain from fine-tuning a judge on median labels is 'mirage-shaped' (concentrated in the Low-consensus stratum under pooled scoring, absent under a matched held-out human) and whether it buys that gain by central-tendency collapse that destroys the base model's free disagreement signal.
hypothesis: Pooled-label SFT raises alpha_pooled mostly on Low-consensus items while HCA/alpha vs a held-out rater stays flat there (mechanism: the median is a denoised target, so the judge learns to track it where raters scatter, which a single human cannot match); the same SFT shrinks predicted-score dispersion (fewer 0/4 predictions than humans) and drops entropy->Low AUROC versus the zero-shot base, i.e. training on the aggregate manufactures the measurement artifact the paper attributes to protocol. Control: SFT on one randomly chosen rater's label per item should give the same HCA but lower alpha_pooled; if instead HCA on Low rises under pooled SFT, the paper's warning against tuning to the aggregate-best score is weakened, which is equally worth reporting.

summary: Learned disagreement or learned smoothing? A two-null attribution test for distributional judges: train a Chen-style KL judge leave-one-rater-out and ask how much of its held-out-rater gain is explained by (N1) a single learned temperature on a point judge and (N2) the mean-conditional variance implied by the bounded Likert scale, leaving an item-specific residual.
hypothesis: Most of the held-out-rater NLL/CRPS improvement of distributional training over point SFT is recovered by temperature scaling plus a mean-conditional null (on 0-4 What/Why scales, variance is largely a function of the median via floor/ceiling effects, e.g. Why=0 items have zero spread by construction), and the item-specific residual on Low-consensus items is near zero; the judge's predicted entropy correlates with the item median, not with rater dispersion once the median is partialled out. If the residual is large, distributional judges genuinely learn per-item disagreement and LORO should become the field's evidence standard, so the result matters either way.
mve: benchmark: Commit messages, 6 leave-one-rater-out folds (train distribution from 5 raters, evaluate on the 6th), 80/20 item split inside each fold; readability (9 raters) as a stress case. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, LoRA; distributional head = KL(p_5raters || q_theta) over score tokens (Chen-style, used only as the object under test). | objective: Distributional judge vs point-SFT judge; nulls fitted on training raters only: N1 temperature-scaled point judge, N2 pmf = empirical P(rater label | predicted median), N3 level marginal; oracle = smoothed 5-rater pmf. | comparison: Attribution share = (NLL_N2 - NLL_dist)/(NLL_N2 - NLL_oracle) per stratum; partial correlation of predicted entropy with 5-rater entropy controlling for median; per-stratum reliability diagrams of predicted P(level) vs held-out-rater frequency (csje_eval.heldout_nll, crps, disagreement_auroc). | metric: Held-out-rater NLL and CRPS per stratum, attribution share, partial correlation, reliability-diagram ECE. | gpu_hours: ~4 (6 LORO folds x 2 judges x ~15 min; nulls are free).

summary: Controlled replication of the Ni 2025 effect on Likert SE judging: train the same base judge with GRPO under three reward families (binary match-the-median, ordinal distance to median, CRPS against the rater pmf) and measure what each does to contested items under a matched held-out human.
hypothesis: A verifiable 'match the median' reward is mode-seeking: it collapses rollout entropy, raises alpha_pooled on Low-consensus items without any HCA gain (RL manufactures the mirage rather than judgment), and lengthens reasoning on contested items without improving held-out-human agreement; an ordinal-distance reward reduces the collapse but not the mirage share; a CRPS reward keeps entropy informative (entropy->Low AUROC near the base) at equal or better HCA. Because the base model is fixed and only the reward varies, a null result (no entropy collapse) would overturn the generalisation of Ni 2025 to Likert quality judging, which is also publishable.

summary: Best-of-n with a pooled-label judge on real multi-rater candidate pools: using the code-summarization benchmark's 6 rated candidates per snippet (5 generators + human-written, all scored by 3 raters) and the commit-message dev-vs-generated pairs, measure whether pooled judges select median-safe artifacts on contested pools and how much of the apparent BoN gain survives a held-out-rater evaluation.
hypothesis: Selecting argmax pooled judge score yields candidates whose human ratings are low-variance and mediocre rather than contested-excellent (median-safe bias); the BoN curve (n=1..6) measured against the pooled median rises faster than the same curve measured against any single held-out rater, with the gap concentrated in contested pools; the selected summaries skew toward longer, content-complete outputs that conciseness-preferring raters penalise (an SE-specific conciseness-vs-completeness trade-off), so per-rater regret is unevenly distributed. If pooled BoN is rater-neutral and the gap is small, that is a reassuring result for LLM-judge-based selection in SE and equally reportable.

summary: Rater fingerprinting: with six fixed commit-message raters and nine fixed readability students, compute each judge's per-rater agreement and severity profile, test whether judges are significantly closer to one human than to the others, whether frontier judges share the same nearest rater, whether pooled-label SFT pushes a judge to the panel centroid ('nobody's judgment'), and whether the High-consensus shortfall is a removable severity offset or genuine rank disagreement.
hypothesis: Off-the-shelf frontier judges have a stable, shared fingerprint (nearest to the most lenient rater on What and the strictest on Why, where floor effects dominate), pooled-SFT collapses the fingerprint to the centroid, and a substantial share of the High-consensus shortfall is a scale-use offset that a monotone per-judge recalibration removes, while the Low stratum shows no removable offset (disagreement is about ranking, not severity). Per-rater LoRA imitation on 640 items generalises to unseen items of the same rater only marginally better than the pooled judge, extending Orlikowski's memorisation finding to SE Likert panels.

summary: Is the readability panel learnable at all? A learnability-ceiling card: compute the oracle held-out-rater agreement (8-rater aggregate vs the 9th), Spearman-Brown extrapolation to k raters, and compare LoRA judge, zero-shot frontier judges and a text-free length/feature baseline in leave-one-rater-out evaluation, then apply the same card to the commit-message and summarization panels for contrast.
hypothesis: On the Scalabrino panel (S=0.14) the oracle ceiling itself is low, a LoRA judge trained on the 8-rater distribution does not beat a snippet-length/feature regressor against the held-out student, and HCA CIs straddle zero: the panel carries too little shared signal to train or rank judges, whereas the commit-message What panel has a high ceiling that judges approach on High-consensus items only. The Spearman-Brown curve gives the number of raters needed for an informative panel, so the negative result is actionable rather than merely null; if the LoRA judge does beat the ceiling-adjusted baseline, readability has a learnable core the pooled score hides.

summary: Replace the n-rater empirical pmf as the judge's training target with its Dirichlet-multinomial (or ordinal) posterior predictive — shrinkage proportional to 1/n with concentration fitted by empirical Bayes — scored with a bounded ordinal proper scoring rule (RPS/CRPS), and show that the benefit of distributional fine-tuning over pooled SFT on contested SE items is a function of panel size n that Chen-style KL plus epsilon-ball smoothing only approximates.
hypothesis: Mechanism: with n=3-9 raters the per-item empirical pmf has at most n support points, so KL/CE to it drives the judge to sampling zeros (overconfident on levels no panelist happened to pick) and fits panel-specific dispersion; the log score is unbounded there, so when the held-out rater lands on a zero-mass level NLL explodes, most often on Low-consensus items. Note that scoring 'against individual rater draws' is mathematically identical to scoring against the empirical pmf for any proper scoring rule, so the fix is not leave-one-rater-out training but (a) the target: the Bayes-correct target for 'what will a held-out rater say' is the posterior predictive (counts + alpha*base)/(n + alpha), whose shrinkage strength falls as 1/n, and (b) the rule: a bounded ordinal rule (RPS) makes adjacent-level mass cheap and cannot blow up. Expected direction: held-out-rater NLL/RPS on Low/Partial strata orders posterior-predictive+RPS > RPS-to-pmf > KL-to-pmf, the gaps shrinking monotonically as training raters are subsampled from 5 to 2 (commit) and 8 to 3 (readability), and the best Chen epsilon growing as n shrinks (epsilon is an n-artifact). On readability (S=0.14) every distributional objective converges to the benchmark's marginal rating distribution ('climatology'), i.e. CRPS skill about 0: a judge can post a good CRPS with zero item information, which only a human-anchored skill score exposes.
mve: Benchmark: commit messages (What and Why, 0-4, 6 raters) first, then summarization (3 raters) and readability (9). Base: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct + LoRA r=16, output = next-token distribution over the score tokens. Objectives: CE-to-median; KL-to-empirical-pmf (Chen without and with epsilon-ball, epsilon swept); RPS-to-empirical-CDF; CE and RPS to the Dirichlet-multinomial posterior predictive with alpha fitted by marginal likelihood over items (base = benchmark marginal, plus an ordinal-smoothed variant). Protocol: leave-one-rater-out x 5-fold items; strata computed from training raters only; additionally subsample training raters n in {2,3,4,5}. Metrics: held-out-rater NLL and RPS per stratum, PIT/reliability-resolution decomposition, HCA per stratum, and a distributional skill score anchored at climatology (0) and the (n-1)-rater panel predictive (1) — the distributional analogue of HCA. Pilot: 3 objectives x n in {2,5} x 1 seed on commit-Why, about 1-2 GPU-h; full grid about 25 GPU-h.
contribution_type: new method + protocol (human-anchored distributional skill score) + empirical finding

If posterior-predictive targets do not help, distributional fine-tuning is just smoothing and the field should stop reporting KL-to-pmf as evidence of learned disagreement.

summary: Fit a rater-effect channel (many-facet Rasch severity + thresholds, or a Dawid-Skene ordinal confusion matrix) jointly with a generative judge that predicts latent item quality, so any rater — including an unseen one whose channel is estimated from a few anchor items — is predicted as latent composed with channel, and use the fitted model to split each Low-consensus stratum into severity-explained and residual (indeterminate) disagreement.
hypothesis: Mechanism: SE panels are few-raters-many-items (3x1163, 6x800, 9x200), the mirror image of dense crowdsourcing, so per-rater channels are well identified (200+ ratings per rater) while per-item pmfs are not (3-9 draws); a latent-truth-plus-channel model therefore has the right inductive bias for this regime and population-pmf matching (Chen-style) the wrong one. Predictions: on commit-message Why and summarization conciseness a large share of Low-consensus variance is rater severity/scale use, so the channel judge beats pooled-pmf training on held-out-rater NLL and HCA there, and a severity-adjusted matched-human reference alpha_ref rises — part of the paper's 'no advantage on contested items' is both judge and human being scored against an uncalibrated rater. On readability the residual term dominates, conditional independence given the latent fails, and the channel model gains nothing: its failure localizes genuine indeterminacy. Orlikowski-style memorization is avoided because a rater is 1-5 channel parameters estimated from anchor items, not an ID embedding trained on all items.
mve: Step 0 (CPU, hours): fit MFRM (ordinal logistic with item location, rater severity, rater thresholds) and an ordinal Dawid-Skene model on all three panels; report the variance decomposition per stratum and criterion (What vs Why; adequacy vs conciseness vs fluency). Step 1: commit messages, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct + LoRA; the judge emits a latent pmf over 0-4; a per-rater channel (severity + thresholds, or a 5x5 stochastic matrix) maps it to each training rater's predicted pmf; loss = sum over the 5 training raters of -log p_r(y_r); channels initialized from Step 0. Test: the held-out rater's channel is estimated from k in {0,10,25,50} anchor items disjoint from test items; prediction = latent composed with channel. Comparisons: CE-to-median, KL-to-pooled-pmf, rater-ID-token conditioning (Orlikowski baseline). Metrics: held-out-rater NLL/RPS and HCA per stratum (raw and severity-transported), Delta_match with severity-adjusted alpha_ref, rater-facet variance share per stratum. Leave-one-rater-out over all 6 raters. About 3-6 GPU-h.
contribution_type: new method + diagnostic (decomposition of contested strata) + protocol refinement (severity-adjusted matched reference)
prior_work: 2606.27578 PEBS: post-hoc per-rater affine calibration of a scalar RM on dense per-rater data, no strata, no SE, no unseen raters — delta: channel inside the judge's training objective, severity-vs-residual decomposition per stratum, anchor-item transport to unseen raters, severity-adjusted matched reference. 2502.20897 Orlikowski: ID-conditioned fine-tunes memorize annotators — delta: a low-dimensional identifiable channel replaces IDs and is tested on unseen raters. 2410.14632 Zhang: Mean-Var / KL RMs with no rater identity — delta: explicit rater channel plus latent. 2312.08358 DPL: hidden context as an unobserved variable — delta: the context is the rater and is made explicit and estimable. 2503.05965 Guerdan: rating indeterminacy as a validation concern — delta: the residual after rater effects operationalizes indeterminacy for training.
so_what: Answers what SE disagreement is made of. If severity dominates, 'escalate all contested items to humans' is too pessimistic and a rater-calibrated judge recovers them at no annotation cost; if residual dominates, the channel model's failure on Low items is a principled detector of indeterminacy. Informative either way, and it corrects the matched-human reference that the paper's protocol depends on.

summary: Test the shape of contested SE disagreement by training three output heads on the same judge — a cumulative-link ordinal head (forced unimodal), a free categorical head (item-level bimodality allowed), and a K-prototype jury head (bimodality tied to rater-stable camps, with an unseen rater's camp inferred from anchor items) — and comparing them on held-out raters per consensus stratum.
hypothesis: Mechanism: a unimodal head can represent uncertainty about the level but not disagreement about the criterion weighting; SE criteria carry explicit trade-offs (conciseness vs completeness in summaries, What vs Why emphasis in commit messages, developer vs student raters), so contested items should be two-camp and camp membership rater-stable within a criterion. Predictions: the unimodal head's held-out-rater NLL penalty concentrates on Low-consensus items (it must spread mass across the valley between camps); the prototype head beats the categorical head on held-out raters once the unseen rater's camp is identified from 20 or fewer anchor items, with K=2 sufficient; on readability and commit-What (floor effects) the unimodal head ties or wins — no camps, just width. Corollary: Mean-Var RMs (Zhang) encode the wrong shape for SE disagreement.
mve: Benchmarks: commit messages and summarization (conciseness and content adequacy). Stage 1 (about 0.5 GPU-h): frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, hidden state at the score position, fit (a) cumulative-link ordinal logistic, (b) softmax, (c) K in {2,3} prototype mixture with per-rater mixing weights on the training raters (5 for commit, 2 for summarization); the held-out rater's mixing weights are estimated from k anchor items. Stage 2 (about 2 GPU-h): the same heads with a LoRA trunk. Metrics: held-out-rater NLL/RPS per stratum, HCA, camp-identification accuracy vs k, AUROC of predicted bimodality for the Low stratum, and a panel bimodality index (from training raters) against which head predictions are scored.
contribution_type: empirical finding (shape of SE disagreement) + diagnostic + method (prototype head with anchor-item camp assignment)

so_what: If camps are rater-stable, Low-consensus is rubric ambiguity rather than noise: report per camp or fix the rubric instead of escalating; if not, escalation stands and categorical heads suffice. Either way it tells reward-model designers which output parameterization SE disagreement requires.

summary: Treat pooled-label judge fine-tuning as learning with instance-dependent label noise and use per-item training dynamics (loss trajectories / area-under-margin) to recover consensus strata without any rater data, and to show that the pooled-label 'Low-stratum win' is manufactured during the memorization phase of training.
hypothesis: Mechanism: networks fit clean, consistent labels early and memorize noisy ones late; from the judge's viewpoint the pooled median of a contested item is a noisy label, so contested items have low area-under-margin and unstable out-of-fold predictions. Predictions: (i) AUM ranks items by 6-rater consensus with AUROC at least 0.7 and complements zero-shot token entropy; (ii) across epochs, pooled-label agreement on the Low stratum keeps rising while HCA against a held-out rater plateaus — the mirage grows with training, so selecting the checkpoint with the best pooled validation score selects the most memorized judge; (iii) early-learning regularization or small-loss filtering lowers pooled Low-stratum scores but leaves HCA unchanged or better. SE-specific failure mode: the Why criterion's floor effects let a majority-class shortcut fit contested items early, so AUM will mislabel some contested Why items as easy.
mve: Commit messages (What, Why), Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct + LoRA, CE to the pooled median (the standard recipe), 5-fold item CV x 3 seeds x 8 epochs, logging per-item loss and margin in-fold and out-of-fold at every epoch. Compare AUM with (a) panel entropy / stratum, (b) zero-shot Qwen entropy, (c) held-out-rater disagreement. At each epoch: pooled-label Low-stratum agreement and HCA vs the held-out human. Variants: early stopping by held-out-rater NLL vs by pooled score; drop the top-20% AUM-noisy items and retrain. Replicate on summarization. About 2-4 GPU-h.
contribution_type: diagnostic (rater-free contested-item detector) + empirical finding (training-side mechanism of the mirage)
prior_work: 2403.02839 Huang: fine-tuned judges behave as task classifiers — delta: what they learn on contested items and when. 2505.12301 Chen: never inspects training dynamics — delta: dynamics explain why pooled SFT looks good on contested items under pooled scoring. 2503.03064 Wang/Zhang/Choi: inference-time token distribution predicts disagreement — delta: a rater-free training-dynamics detector that needs no multi-rater data. 2403.00409 rDPO / 2404.04102 ROPO / 2407.07880 Dr.DPO: noise-robust PO with a scalar flip rate — delta: per-instance dynamics on real multi-rater data, separating plurality from noise. 2510.22954 Artificial Hivemind: miscalibration where annotators diverge, diagnostic only — delta: a training-side mechanism.
so_what: Provides a way to flag contested items in the many single-rater SE benchmarks, and a training-side explanation of the mirage that turns the paper's warning against tuning to the aggregate-best score into a measurable checkpoint-selection bias; a null result (no separation) would indicate contested items are systematically learnable camps rather than noise, which feeds MT3.

summary: Use the judge's predicted rater distribution for risk-sensitive candidate selection (lower quantile / CVaR / P(rating >= tau) instead of expected rating) in best-of-n over SE artifacts and measure, with real held-out human ratings per consensus stratum, whether mean-seeking selection sacrifices the strictest rater on contested items.
hypothesis: Mechanism: a mean or median selector picks the candidate that pleases the median rater; where raters split, that candidate can be rated low by a minority camp, whereas a CVaR selector picks the candidate no rater rates badly — the selection-time version of preference collapse. Predictions: on contested pairs CVaR selection raises the minimum held-out-rater rating and the fraction of raters rating at least 2, at small or zero cost in mean rating; on High-consensus pairs the rules coincide. SE twist: generated commit messages are 'safe' (What-complete) and developer messages 'risky' (terse but Why-rich), so the rules should disagree mostly on Why, and the direction of the disagreement is itself a finding.
mve: Commit-message benchmark: 400 diffs x 2 candidates (developer vs generated) x 6 ratings gives 400 selection problems with real human outcomes and no generation. Judge pmfs: zero-shot Qwen2.5-Coder-7B score-token distribution, the frontier judges' 3 sampled runs, and fine-tuned judges from MT1/MT2. Rules: argmax mean, median, CVaR_0.25, P(>=3). Outcome: the chosen candidate's rating by each held-out rater (excluded from strata), reported as mean, min-over-raters and fraction below 2, by pair consensus, vs oracle (pooled human) and random. About 0.5 GPU-h. Extension: summarization if multiple summaries per snippet exist; Qwen3-14B generating n=8 commit messages with frontier-judge outcomes as a secondary check.
contribution_type: empirical finding (downstream consequence) + method (drop-in selection rule)
prior_work: 2506.19248 HedgeTune / 2503.21878 / 2604.04648: best-of-n under an imperfect or uncertain reward model — delta: uncertainty is across human raters, outcomes are real multi-rater ratings, reported per stratum. 2409.10164 QRM: quantile RM that mentions risk-aware use — delta: evaluated against held-out humans on ordinal SE data. 2405.16455 Xiao / 2511.08594 Slocum: preference collapse on synthetic groups — delta: first measurement on real panels at the selection step. 2410.14632 Zhang: no downstream experiment — delta: downstream selection.
so_what: Tells SE teams whether aggregating reward by the mean silently sacrifices minority reviewers on contested artifacts; a null result is reassuring (contested-item measurement problems do not propagate to selection), a positive result is a drop-in selection rule that needs no retraining.

summary: Calibrate conformal prediction sets for Likert judges against a random held-out rater (exchangeability over rater x item pairs) rather than the pooled label, quantify the resulting 'coverage mirage' per consensus stratum, and train the judge with a rater-exchangeable conformal set-size loss so that set width becomes an escalation signal validated against a matched human.
hypothesis: Mechanism: a coverage guarantee against the pooled median is not a guarantee against any human; on Low-consensus items the median is a denoised target, so sets calibrated on it under-cover real raters by roughly the panel's within-item dispersion. Calibrating on rater draws restores 1-alpha coverage but widens sets exactly on contested items, so width inflation is a per-benchmark measure of the mirage (small on summarization, large on commit-Why, extreme on readability) and set width a validated disagreement predictor. Conformal training (set-size regularizer under the rater-exchangeable threshold) shrinks High-stratum sets without losing Low coverage, improving the cost-quality Pareto of a route-to-human policy scored against a matched human.
mve: Phase 1 (no training, CPU): existing judge outputs (Qwen pmf, frontier judges' 3 runs, fine-tuned judges) on all three benchmarks; split conformal with nonconformity 1-q(y) and an ordinal cumulative variant, calibrated (i) on the pooled median, (ii) on rater draws; report coverage vs a held-out rater per stratum, set-size AUROC for the Low stratum, and the Pareto of (fraction escalated, HCA of non-escalated items) vs the matched human. Phase 2 (about 2 GPU-h): Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct + LoRA on commit messages with CE plus a differentiable conformal set-size loss under rater-draw calibration; same metrics.
contribution_type: protocol (rater-exchangeable coverage) + empirical finding (coverage mirage) + method (conformal training for routing)

summary: Map the annotation-budget frontier (items n x raters k) for training a distributional SE judge on small ordinal panels: at fixed budget n*k, when do extra raters beat extra items, and below which k does 'learned disagreement' collapse into 'pooled label + global smoothing' under a held-out-rater, consensus-stratified evaluation?
hypothesis: Two axes control two strata. High-stratum HCA is a function of n only (more items), while Low-stratum held-out-rater CRPS/NLL and entropy->Low AUROC improve only with k and only above a threshold k*~4-5: at k<=3 (the most common SE regime, e.g. Crupi et al.) the empirical pmf is dominated by multinomial sampling noise, so soft-CE to the empirical pmf is statistically indistinguishable from median-CE plus a global temperature. Empirical-Bayes / ordinal-smoothed targets (Dirichlet shrinkage toward the criterion prior, leave-one-rater-out CRPS) recover part of the gap at small k. The evaluation floor itself also moves with k: the oracle held-out-rater CRPS (pmf of the other k-1 raters scored against the held-out one, the distributional analogue of alpha_ref) degrades as k falls, so a 3-rater benchmark cannot certify disagreement learning.
mve: benchmark: Commit messages (800 msgs x 6 raters, What+Why, diffs) as the main grid; code readability (200 x 9) as the dense-panel replicate; code summarization (3 raters) as the k=3 boundary case. Grouped split by commit hash / function: 600 train / 200 test items on CM (rater 6 always held out from training; strata and HCA on test items use the full panel, no leakage). | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, LoRA r=16 on score-token logits (next-token distribution over '0'..'4' is already informative out of the box; 0.7 s/item, 16 GB). | objective: Four targets: (1) median-CE (pooled SFT), (2) soft-CE/KL to empirical pmf of the k training raters (Chen-style core, no adversarial ball), (3) ordinal CRPS/EMD to the empirical CDF, (4) Dirichlet-shrunk pmf (beta toward criterion-level prior, beta picked by leave-one-rater-out CRPS on train). | comparison: Grid n in {75,150,300,600} x k in {1,2,3,5} x 4 targets x 3 seeds (192 runs) on CM; n in {50,100,150} x k in {2,4,8} on readability (hold out 1 rater); iso-budget curves (n*k = const) and per-axis learning curves. Report the oracle held-out-rater CRPS floor as a function of k alongside. | metric: Held-out-rater (rater 6) NLL and CRPS vs the held-out rating; HCA by High/Partial/Low (point = median of predicted pmf) with bootstrap CI; Delta_match; entropy->Low-stratum AUROC; crossover k* where target (2)/(4) beats (1) on Low-stratum held-out-rater CRPS with CI excluding 0. | gpu_hours: ~30 (CM: 192 LoRA runs x ~6 min + 200-item evals) + ~6 (readability) = ~36 GPU-h across 4 GPUs; 1-2 GPU-h pilot = k in {2,5} x n in {150,600} x targets (1),(2), 1 seed, Why criterion.
contribution_type: empirical finding + protocol (annotation-budget guidance and a held-out-rater CRPS floor for small panels)
risk: MEDIUM (200 test items per split may leave Low-stratum CIs wide; mitigate by pooling What/Why, repeated grouped splits, and paired bootstrap across targets)
prior_work: 2505.12301: Chen et al. fix 5 raters and evaluate on the same pooled distribution; we vary k and n, hold out a rater, stratify, and show where their target degenerates to smoothing. ; 2410.14632: Diverging Preferences trains on fixed 3-5 rater panels with no budget axis and no held-out-annotator reference. ; 2606.27578: PEBS is post-hoc per-rater calibration needing per-rater held-out data; we ask the upstream question of how many raters a distributional target needs at all. ; 2605.11865: Variance-aware RM flags identifiability of per-item variance from few raters as open; we measure it empirically with k-subsampling on real SE panels. ; 2511.14117: Soft-label training is advocated with fixed dense panels; we give the rater-count learning curve and its floor. ; 2502.20897: We adopt unseen-rater evaluation (the failure mode Orlikowski et al. found) as the primary metric rather than a per-annotator model. ; 2510.22954: Artificial Hivemind uses 25 ratings/item; we cover the 2-9 rater regime SE actually has.

summary: Test-time compute vs training: sample N in {1..32} CoT judgments from untrained 7B/14B/frontier judges, treat the sample histogram as a 'free' rating distribution, and measure the exchange rate against a LoRA judge trained on n disaggregated items under held-out-rater CSJE -- testing whether majority-voting over samples manufactures the alignment mirage.
hypothesis: (H1) Self-consistency voting is an aggregation step: as N grows, agreement with the pooled median rises monotonically on Low-consensus items while HCA against a matched held-out human stays flat or falls -- the paper's aggregation confound reproduced by test-time compute alone. (H2) The sample histogram carries model (epistemic) uncertainty, not rater dispersion: its entropy->Low AUROC saturates by N~8 at a level below a judge trained on >=150 disaggregated items, and the zero-CoT next-token distribution (N=infinity, one forward pass) is at least as good, consistent with the finding that judge panels behave like ~2 independent votes. (H3) Exchange rate: 32 samples (32x inference cost) buy less held-out-rater CRPS than ~150 training items; thinking mode on Qwen3-14B does not close the gap on Low items.
mve: benchmark: Commit messages, 800 items x What/Why; 200-item subset for frontier top-up. Reuse existing 3-run frontier outputs (Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5) as N=3 anchors and CodeVisionary/SE-Jury runs as multi-agent anchors. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-14B (thinking on/off, capped budget) via vLLM at T=1; trained comparator = 7B LoRA soft-CE/CRPS judge at n in {100,300,600} (from the iso-budget pilot). | objective: No training for the sampling arm; for each N form (a) sample pmf, (b) majority/median vote point, (c) mean-of-samples point; plus (d) zero-CoT score-token distribution. | comparison: Sampled-ensemble curves over N vs trained-judge curves over n on the same test items; per-model, per-criterion; thinking on vs off on the 14B; frontier N=3 -> N=8 on the 200-item subset via OpenRouter. | metric: alpha vs pooled median by stratum (mirage check), HCA by stratum vs held-out human, held-out-rater CRPS/NLL of the sample pmf, entropy->Low AUROC; the exchange-rate curve N(n) where sampled CRPS equals trained CRPS. | gpu_hours: ~2 (7B: 800 x 2 x 32 samples x ~250 tokens with prefix caching) + ~8 (14B thinking, capped) + ~2 trained-judge evals = ~12 GPU-h; ~$20 API for the frontier top-up. 1-2 GPU-h pilot: 7B, N<=16, 400 items, Why only.
contribution_type: empirical finding + diagnostic (a 'self-consistency mirage' test any judge paper can run)
risk: LOW (either outcome is informative: either test-time sampling is a cheap substitute for disaggregated training, or it is shown to inflate pooled scores without matched-human gains)
prior_work: 2407.18370: Trust-or-Escalate uses simulated-annotator sampling for abstention guarantees against a pooled label; we score the same sampling against a held-out human by stratum and compare it to training, without abstention. ; 2503.03064: Wang/Zhang/Choi show judgment distributions beat greedy and predict pairwise disagreement (inference-only, NLP); we add the N-sample axis, Likert SE, held-out-rater scoring, and a trained comparator. ; 2504.02495: DeepSeek-GRM scales inference by voting against gold labels; we test whether voting is aggregation that inflates pooled agreement on contested items. ; 2605.29800: Nine Judges shows panels of different judges ~2 independent votes; we test the same collapse for samples of one judge and price it against training. ; 2608.07517: Vote-margin abstention at 49% coverage is scored against one label; we do not abstain and use the matched human as reference. ; 2505.12301: Chen et al. compare trained judges only to greedy untuned GPT-4o; we give the full test-time-compute baseline they omit. ; 2506.19467: Ni et al. find RLVR reasoning hurts disagreement modelling on NLP classification; our thinking on/off arm is a Likert-SE data point but the main axis is N, not reasoning training.

summary: Output-parameterisation regime for small ordinal panels: with the same 7B backbone and data, compare a 5-way score-token categorical, a 2-parameter cumulative-link (ordered-logit) head, a Gaussian mean-variance head, and a verbalized rater-count histogram ('of 6 developers: 1:3, 2:3') as the judge's distributional output, sweeping training raters k in {2,3,5} and panels (3/6/9 raters).
hypothesis: Bias-variance in the output head: the per-item degrees of freedom should scale with rater count. A 5-way categorical (4 free params/item) overfits a k<=3 empirical pmf and hallucinates dispersion, so the 2-dof cumulative-link head wins held-out-rater CRPS on CS (k=3) and at subsampled k<=3 on CM, while at k=9 (readability) the categorical catches up. The verbalized count histogram is the only head that can express a bimodal split (e.g. 3-3 on Why) and will have the best Low-stratum AUROC iff SE disagreement is bimodal (two camps: conciseness vs completeness) rather than dispersed -- a property we measure directly from the panels (fraction of items whose empirical pmf is bimodal).
mve: benchmark: Commit messages (6 raters, What/Why) with rater subsampling k in {2,3,5}; code summarization (3 raters, CA/Conciseness/Fluency); readability (9 raters) as the dense anchor. Grouped splits by hash/function. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct + LoRA r=16; heads A-C read the last hidden state at the score position, head D is plain SFT on a count string. | objective: A: soft-CE to empirical pmf over score tokens; B: ordered-logit (mu, log sigma) trained by NLL of every individual rating (structured soft-CE); C: Gaussian NLL on ratings (Mean-Var analogue), discretised to bins for CRPS; D: token CE on the verbalized rater-count histogram, decoded greedily and with 8 samples. | comparison: 4 heads x 3 k x 2 benchmarks x 3 seeds = 72 runs, plus readability at k in {4,8}; also compare each head's point prediction (pmf median) against a median-CE point judge. | metric: Held-out-rater CRPS and NLL (primary), HCA by stratum, entropy->Low AUROC, calibration of predicted dispersion vs held-out-panel dispersion; bimodality rate of panels vs bimodality rate of predictions. | gpu_hours: ~8 training + ~4 eval = ~12 GPU-h; 1-2 GPU-h pilot: heads A vs B vs D on CM Why at k=5, 1 seed.
contribution_type: new method (cumulative-link / count-histogram judge heads for Likert panels) + empirical finding (dof-vs-rater-count law, bimodality test)
risk: MEDIUM (head differences may be small on High items; the Low-stratum and k<=3 regimes are where the claim lives, and CIs there are wider)
prior_work: 2505.12301: Chen et al. use only the categorical score-token head with KL; we show its per-item dof is mis-sized for 3-6 rater panels and offer the ordinal 2-dof alternative. ; 2510.00263: Li et al. verbalize binary probabilities fitted to synthetic persona annotators; we verbalize ordinal rater counts fitted to real 6- and 9-developer panels and score them against a held-out rater. ; 2410.14632: Diverging Preferences' Mean-Var RM is a Gaussian scalar RM on pairwise pooled accuracy; we put the head inside a generative judge, use an ordinal link, and test head choice against panel size. ; 2409.10164: QRM outputs quantiles for pairwise reward models; ours is pointwise Likert with a held-out-rater proper score. ; 2509.18658: Conformal intervals for Likert judges are post-hoc; our dispersion is learned and scored against panel dispersion. ; 2603.17145: REAL is point regression with correlation rewards; we predict a distribution and ask how many parameters it should have. ; 2605.25296: Mokhova et al. observe LLM Likert distributions are polarised vs humans; our bimodality rate quantifies the target-side structure in SE panels.
so_what: Gives a concrete design rule for anyone building a distributional SE judge on the panels that actually exist (3-9 raters): choose the output head by rater count, and use the count-histogram form when disagreement is two-camp rather than diffuse.

summary: Criterion regime as a natural experiment: compute, from the annotator matrix alone, a split-half reliability of per-item disagreement (is disagreement an item property or a rater property?) for every criterion (CM What/Why x developer/generated, CS CA/Conciseness/Fluency, readability), use it as a pre-training ceiling on any judge's entropy->Low AUROC, then verify with distributional LoRA training that the gain over pooled SFT tracks this ceiling rather than the criterion's contested mass.
hypothesis: Contested mass is necessary but not sufficient for disagreement-aware training to pay off. Readability has the most Low-consensus items but a split-half disagreement reliability near 0 (disagreement is rater-level scale/style, removable by per-rater z-scoring), so distributional training yields no Low-stratum gain; CM Why has high contested mass and a reliable item-level disagreement signal (the Why floor effect is diff-dependent), so it yields the largest gain; CS Conciseness shows a moderate item-level signal (the conciseness-vs-completeness trade-off is a property of the summary) despite only 3 raters. The ceiling computed before training predicts the post-training AUROC within its CI; per-rater affine pre-calibration raises the ceiling where disagreement is scale-driven and leaves it unchanged where it is ambiguity-driven.
mve: benchmark: All three benchmarks; split-half analysis needs k>=6 (CM: all 10 disjoint 3+3 rater splits; readability: 4+5 splits), CS (k=3) only admits 1-vs-2 splits and is reported as the uninformative boundary. | base_model: CPU-only for the ceiling; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct + LoRA for the verification arm. | objective: Ceiling: Spearman correlation across items of per-item dispersion (range/variance/entropy) between disjoint rater halves, Spearman-Brown corrected to full panel; repeat after per-rater z-scoring (PEBS-style scale removal). Training: median-CE vs soft-CE/CRPS LoRA per criterion. | comparison: Six criteria x 2 objectives x 3 seeds (36 runs); regress the Low-stratum held-out-rater CRPS gain and entropy->Low AUROC on (contested mass, split-half reliability, discriminative power S). | metric: Split-half reliability r_sh with bootstrap CI; post-training entropy->Low AUROC vs the r_sh-implied ceiling; Low-stratum held-out-rater CRPS gain; HCA by stratum. | gpu_hours: ~0 for the ceiling (minutes on CPU) + ~5 GPU-h for verification; the pilot is CPU-only and can run today.
contribution_type: diagnostic + empirical finding (a learnability ceiling for disagreement-aware judging, computable from the annotator matrix before training)
risk: LOW (the ceiling is a contribution whether it is high or low; the verification arm is cheap)
prior_work: 2410.14632: Diverging Preferences reports a Diverging-ID AUROC without asking whether divergence is predictable from the item at all; we supply the ceiling and the SE instances. ; 2510.22954: Artificial Hivemind documents judge failure where 25 raters diverge; we separate item-level from rater-level divergence and do it in the 3-9 rater regime. ; 2606.27578: PEBS shows pooling confounds rater scale with reward; we use per-rater scale removal as the tool that splits the ceiling into scale vs ambiguity components. ; 2605.01168: The opposition index predicts rating variance from text on NLP data; we bound how predictable variance can be and test it on SE criteria. ; 2503.05965: Rating indeterminacy validation is framework-level; ours is a one-number diagnostic per criterion tied to a trained judge. ; 2604.08425: DiADEM predicts who disagrees using demographics; SE panels have no demographics, so we ask the prior question of whether disagreement is an item property. ; 2505.12301: Chen et al. report KL gains per dataset without a learnability reference; our ceiling would tell whether their SummEval gain is item-level structure or smoothing.
so_what: Before anyone trains a disagreement-aware SE judge (or reviews a paper claiming one), a few minutes on the annotator matrix says whether there is any item-level disagreement to learn, which criteria are worth it, and how much of the 'disagreement' is just rater scale.

summary: Downstream best-of-n on real multi-rater candidate sets (code summarization: 98 Java + 99 Python functions x 5-6 candidate summaries from human/GPT-4/GPT-3.5/CodeLlama-7/13/34B, every candidate rated by the same 3 raters; commit messages: 400 diffs x {developer, generated} x 6 raters): does a pooled-label judge's selection become median-seeking as n grows from 2 to 6, measured as held-out-rater regret split by contested vs uncontested functions?
hypothesis: At n=2-3 pooled and distributional judges select the same candidate; by n>=5 the pooled judge increasingly selects candidates with low panel variance (bland, consensual summaries), so held-out-rater regret on contested functions plateaus from n~3 while it keeps falling on uncontested ones; selection by consensus-likelihood P(rating>=4) or a lower quantile of the predicted pmf trades a little uncontested regret for lower contested regret and higher minority satisfaction (fraction of raters whose personal best is within 1 point of the pick). Median-seeking appears as a monotone fall in the selected candidate's panel variance with n, absent for rater-optimal selection.
mve: benchmark: Code summarization (CA, Conciseness, Fluency; subsets of the 5-6 candidates give n in {2..6}, all subsets enumerated) and commit messages (n=2, developer vs generated). Judges trained out-of-fold with 5-fold grouped CV by function/hash so every candidate is scored by a judge that never saw its function. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct: untrained score-token distribution, LoRA median-CE (pooled), LoRA soft-CE/CRPS (distributional); existing frontier point outputs (Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5) as zero-training anchors. | objective: Selection rules: argmax point score; argmax predicted mean; argmax P(>=4); argmax lower quantile (pessimistic); random (floor); per-rater oracle and pooled-median oracle (ceilings). | comparison: BoN curves over n for each judge x rule, stratified by the candidate set's contestedness (mean Low-fraction of its panels); generator fixed effects to control for bland-generator confounds. | metric: Held-out-rater regret = mean over raters r of [max_c H_r(c) - H_r(selected)]; minority satisfaction; win-rate vs human_written; panel variance of the selected candidate vs n; all with function-level bootstrap CIs. | gpu_hours: ~6 (5 folds x 2 trained judges x 3 seeds on ~2.8k CS examples) + ~3 (CM) + ~1 scoring = ~10 GPU-h. 1-2 GPU-h pilot: untrained 7B token distribution vs frontier point judges on CS Java BoN curves, no training.
contribution_type: empirical finding + protocol (held-out-rater regret as the matched-human analogue for selection)
risk: MEDIUM (n<=6 may be too small for pooled and distributional selection to diverge; bland-candidate effects may be confounded with generator identity -- controlled by fixed effects; extension to n=32 needs fresh generations plus a 3-rater mini-panel on ~100 functions)
effort: 2-3 weeks (plus ~1 week of annotation for the n=32 extension)
prior_work: 2410.14632: Diverging Preferences stops at reward-model accuracy; we measure what the pooled vs distributional signal does to selection on real multi-rater candidate sets. ; 2506.19248: HedgeTune studies BoN with an imperfect proxy against a single gold reward; our 'gold' is a panel of raters and regret is matched to a held-out one. ; 2604.04648: BoN pessimism motivates lower-quantile selection theoretically; we test it against held-out humans on SE artifacts. ; 2503.21878: Is-BoN-best compares selection strategies under one reward; we split by contestedness. ; 2409.06691: GAPO consumes soft pairwise labels that are synthetic; our soft signal comes from real 3- and 6-rater SE panels and we measure the downstream split. ; 2405.16455: Preference-collapse theory predicts majority amplification; this is its first measurement on real raters in SE generation. ; 2511.08594: Soft Preference Learning shows majority overweighting on synthetic groups; we show whether it appears at n<=6 with real developer panels. ; 2608.10126: PA-RLHF documents averaging-induced majority dominance in RLHF; our setting is selection, where the effect should emerge as a function of n. ; 2403.09032: CodeUltraFeedback optimises code LLMs against a single pooled GPT-3.5 judge; we show what that pooled signal selects on contested items.
so_what: Best-of-n with an LLM judge is the cheapest deployment of SE judges; this shows whether it quietly optimises for the median rater and where (contested items, larger n) a distributional or pessimistic selection rule is worth its cost.

summary: Judge-size regime with training as the intervention: does a 7B judge LoRA-trained on <=600 disaggregated SE ratings match or beat 70B and 2026 frontier point judges on the High stratum under HCA, and does any axis (parameters 7B->14B->70B->frontier, or training) move the Low-stratum HCA at all -- yielding a cost-per-HCA Pareto by stratum?
hypothesis: (H1) High stratum: a trained 7B reaches HCA within CI of the frontier judges (near 1) at ~1/100 the per-item cost, because High items are learnable from a few hundred examples (fine-tuned judges behave like task classifiers). (H2) Low stratum: HCA is flat in parameters and flat in training -- no configuration's CI separates from the held-out-human anchor -- showing the stratum, not the model, is the binding constraint (consistent with the paper's F4 and with a low item-level learnability ceiling). (H3) Pooled-label agreement tells the opposite story (trained judges and frontier 'win' on Low), so the cost-Pareto drawn with pooled alpha picks a different judge than the one drawn with HCA.
mve: benchmark: Commit messages (main) and code summarization; same grouped test split as the iso-budget study so 7B runs are reused. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (untrained / LoRA median-CE / LoRA soft-CE-CRPS), Qwen3-14B (same three; QLoRA 4-bit or 2-GPU sharding since 14B bf16 exceeds the ~22 GB free per card), released 70B-class zero-shot outputs (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, QwQ-32B), frontier runs (Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5) and CodeVisionary / SE-Jury. | objective: Median-CE vs soft-CE/CRPS LoRA at n=600 for the two local models; no training for the larger models. | comparison: Parameter axis x training axis on one plot per stratum with measured cost per item (local GPU-seconds, API price); paired bootstrap vs the held-out-human anchor. | metric: HCA by stratum with CI and S; pooled alpha by stratum (to show the Pareto flips); Delta_match; held-out-rater CRPS for the distributional configs. | gpu_hours: ~3 (14B QLoRA, 6 runs) + ~3 (14B evals at ~1.5 s/item) + reuse of 7B runs = ~8 GPU-h; 1-2 GPU-h pilot: 7B trained vs frontier existing outputs on CM, no new API calls.
contribution_type: empirical finding (a stratum-wise cost-HCA Pareto; extends the paper's F4 from scaling to training)
risk: LOW-MEDIUM (H1 likely; H2 is a null that is informative either way; the 14B arm is optional if memory is tight)
prior_work: 2403.02839: Huang et al. show fine-tuned judges act as task classifiers that do not generalise; we show where that is enough (High stratum) and where nothing helps (Low), against a matched human. ; 2505.12301: Chen et al. compare 7-8B trained judges to untuned GPT-4o on pooled KL; we compare across sizes under a stratified, matched-human metric with cost. ; 2505.20854: SE-Jury ensembles strong judges against pooled labels with an IAA ceiling; we place it on the stratum-wise Pareto against a trained small judge. ; 2507.16587: Crupi et al. evaluate off-the-shelf judges on pooled CS labels; we add trained small judges and the HCA view. ; 2410.13341: Dorner et al. bound what a judge can add to evaluation; our Pareto gives the empirical SE counterpart by stratum. ; 2407.18370: Trust-or-Escalate cascades cheap->strong LLMs; our result says the strong end of the cascade buys nothing on Low items under a matched-human reference, so escalation should target humans.

summary: Use the code-summarization benchmark as a ready-made best-of-n testbed (CS-Java: 98 functions x 6 already-rated candidates = CodeLlama-7B/13B/34B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4-turbo, human-written; CS-Python: 126 functions x up to 6; CM: 400 diffs x {developer, generated} as best-of-2) and ask whether selecting by the judge's expected score, lower quantile, P(score>=4), or mode changes the quality the *selected* artifact receives from a held-out human, separately on contested vs uncontested pools.
hypothesis: On uncontested pools every rule ties. On contested pools (the three raters' top picks differ), (i) even a perfect pooled-median oracle selector loses to a matched human selector when scored by a held-out rater, i.e. optimising the denoised aggregate is not optimal for any individual (the mirage has a downstream cost), and (ii) expected-score selection tracks the pooled oracle, while lower-quantile ('fewest objectors') selection does better on Conciseness (the trade-off criterion) and no better on Content Adequacy. Mechanism: the pooled expectation is maximised by hedged candidates no rater dislikes, which on trade-off criteria are candidates no rater rates top. Publishable either way: a null result means distributional judges have no best-of-n payoff in SE and stratified reporting is the whole story.
mve: benchmark: CS-Java (594 items, 98 pools of 6, 3 raters, CA/Conciseness/Fluency) + CS-Python pools with >=4 candidates; CM 400 diffs as best-of-2 on What/Why with 6 raters. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct zero-shot score-token distribution (verbatim Crupi/Zeng prompts) and Qwen3-14B; existing 3-run Opus 4.8 / Gemini 3.1 Pro / GPT-5.5 outputs treated as 3-sample empirical distributions; optional LoRA pair: pooled-median SFT judge vs leave-one-rater-out soft-target judge, 5-fold by function. | objective: No training needed for the pilot. Selection rules per pool: argmax E[s], argmax q_0.25, argmax P(s>=4), argmax mode, random; oracles: pooled-median oracle and per-rater oracle; matched-human selector = held-out rater h picking by their own ratings. | comparison: For each pool and each evaluating rater r (3 folds), rating given by r to the candidate chosen by each rule/selector; pools stratified as contested (raters' top sets disjoint or pool range >=2) vs uncontested. Judge selector vs matched-human selector vs pooled oracle, same rater r. | metric: Mean held-out-rater rating of the selected candidate; P(selected is in rater r's top set); regret vs per-rater oracle; HCA-style normalisation (rule - random)/(human-selector - random); bootstrap CIs over pools; per-criterion and per-stratum. | est_gpu_hours: <=1 for the zero-shot pilot (about 3.5k forward passes on a 7B); +2 for the LoRA judge pair.
contribution_type: empirical finding + protocol (CSJE transplanted to selection)
prior_work: 2506.19248: HedgeTune studies best-of-n under an imperfect proxy reward against one gold reward; here the 'gold' is itself plural and the selected artifact is scored by a matched held-out human by consensus stratum. ; 2503.21878: Best-of-n analysis against a single true reward; no multi-rater data, no contested/uncontested split, no human selector baseline. ; 2410.14632: Diverging Preferences trains distributional RMs but has no downstream selection experiment; we measure what the distribution buys at selection time. ; 2505.12301: Distributional judge evaluated only by KL to the same pooled pmf; we evaluate the decision the distribution drives, on SE pools, against a held-out rater. ; 2507.16587: Crupi et al. rate all six generators but pool ratings and never use the pools as candidate sets; we reuse their ratings as an oracle-labelled best-of-n benchmark with zero new annotation.
so_what: First measurement of what a pooled-optimal selector costs each individual reader of a summary, entirely offline on existing SE ratings, yielding a concrete selection-rule recommendation (expected score vs lower quantile) for SE generation pipelines that use an LLM judge as the picker.

summary: Treat the judge's aggregation rule (expected score vs lower quantile vs full distribution) as the experimental treatment: build DPO pairs / best-of-n picks from n=8 sampled commit messages per diff using a pooled-point judge versus a distributional judge, fine-tune Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and measure whether the pooled signal collapses per-diff output variance and Why-rationale specificity specifically on diffs whose benchmark messages were Low-consensus, with a held-out-human check on a small sample.
hypothesis: Pooled-signal optimisation converges to hedged, median-pleasing messages (moderate length, generic rationale such as 'to improve readability') and removes the tails (terse one-liners, detailed rationale), and this collapse is concentrated on contested diffs; the lower-quantile rule preserves spread without hurting uncontested quality. Mechanism: the expected pooled score is maximised by candidates that no rater dislikes, which on contested criteria (Why, Conciseness) are compromise artifacts; on uncontested diffs both rules pick the same candidate. If no collapse appears, the theoretical preference-collapse literature does not transfer to small-panel SE generation, itself a useful negative.
mve: benchmark: CM 400 diffs (git_diff_u3 available), What/Why, 6 raters; contested diff = its developer or generated message sits in the Low stratum on Why; 5-fold by diff. | base_model: Policy: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct (LoRA). Judges: (a) pooled-point judge = same backbone LoRA-SFT'd on the 6-rater median; (b) distributional judge = LoRA-SFT'd with leave-one-rater-out soft targets (pilot: zero-shot score-token distribution). | objective: Sample 8 messages/diff (T=0.8); construct pairs (max vs min) by expected score [pooled] or by q_0.25 [distributional]; LoRA-DPO 2 epochs on 320 diffs; also GAPO soft-label DPO with p from the distributional judge as an existing-method baseline; best-of-8 variant without training as a control. | comparison: Base policy vs DPO-pooled vs DPO-quantile vs GAPO-soft vs BoN-pooled vs BoN-quantile, generated on 80 held-out diffs per fold, split by contested vs uncontested diffs. | metric: Label-free: per-diff length std, self-BLEU, distinct-2 across 8 samples, Why-rationale presence rate and genericity (judge-detected), predicted-score entropy; human check: 3 raters x 120 messages (40 contested + 40 uncontested diffs x 3 systems) scored under the held-out-rater protocol; frontier-judge scores reported only with the CSJE caveat. | est_gpu_hours: about 4 total (sampling 0.3, judge scoring 1, 5-fold LoRA-DPO 2.5); single-fold pilot about 1.5.
