summary: Build the cost-quality Pareto of a hybrid evaluator that routes a fraction f of items to a held-out human and leaves the rest to the judge, scored against a matched held-out rater by consensus stratum, and compare routing policies: judge spread/entropy (HyPAC/Gupta style), predicted Low stratum, a learned per-item gain head trained on leave-one-rater-out residuals, random, and oracle gain.
hypothesis: Under a matched-human target, entropy routing is nearly useless: on Low-consensus items a human is no better than the judge (paper F2), so routing them buys little, while the judge's real shortfall sits on High/Partial items that entropy routing keeps. A gain-trained router Pareto-dominates entropy routing, and the optimal routing set is anti-correlated with judge uncertainty on Why. Mechanism: the per-item value of a human equals alpha_ref minus alpha_judge, which the paper shows is largest where consensus is high. Publishable either way: if entropy routing wins, the High-consensus shortfall is not exploitable by routing.
mve: benchmark: CM 800 messages x What/Why (6 raters; one rater is the routed 'human', another the reference, rotate all pairs); CS-Java (3 raters) and CoReEval readability (9 raters) as secondary panels. | base_model: Existing judge outputs: released GPT-4 few-shot CoT, the 3-run frontier outputs (Opus 4.8 / Gemini 3.1 Pro / GPT-5.5), CodeVisionary / SE-Jury, plus Qwen2.5-Coder-7B score-token distributions (10 min). | objective: Routing policies P1 judge entropy / score spread; P2 predicted-Low-stratum-first; P3 learned gain head (logistic/GBM on entropy, score, message length, diff size, criterion) trained to predict per-item human-minus-judge agreement from leave-one-rater-out residuals, cross-validated by item; P4 random; P5 oracle gain. | comparison: Hybrid HCA(f) curves for f in {0, 0.1, ..., 1} per policy and per judge; per-stratum decomposition of the gain; cost counted as routed fraction. | metric: HCA(f) vs matched rater; area under the HCA-f curve; f needed to reach HCA=0.9; overlap between entropy-routed and oracle-routed sets; bootstrap CIs over items and rater pairs. | est_gpu_hours: <=0.5 (all offline on existing judge outputs).
contribution_type: protocol + diagnostic + empirical finding
prior_work: 2407.18370: Trust-or-Escalate guarantees agreement with a pooled label and escalates to a stronger LLM; our endpoint is a human, the target is a matched held-out rater, and we show where routing actually pays by stratum. ; 2602.02550: HyPAC's human tier is thresholded on calibrated uncertainty against one gold label; we test whether uncertainty is even the right routing key once the target is a matched human. ; 2602.13110: SCOPE abstains to bound pairwise error vs gold; no human cost model, no stratified gain decomposition. ; 2604.15302: Gupta proposes conformal set width as a human-review trigger; we compare that trigger against a learned gain head under CSJE. ; 2310.15638: CoAnnotating allocates human vs LLM work by LLM uncertainty against gold labels for classification; we do SE Likert judging with a matched-human target. ; 2410.13341: Dorner et al. bound judge-based debiasing vs ground truth; our quantity is agreement with a peer rater, where no ground truth exists.
so_what: Turns the paper's measurement result into an operational rule for hybrid SE evaluation budgets: which items to send to humans, at what cost, and why the default 'escalate the uncertain ones' may be exactly backwards once judges are scored on a human's footing.

summary: Train a generative Likert judge with GRPO under four rewards: hard median match (JudgeLRM/REAL-style RLVR), random-rater match, per-rater CRPS of the judge's verbalised 5-bin distribution against a freshly drawn training rater each rollout (a proper scoring rule that is unbiased for the rater pmf), and CRPS plus an entropy ablation for hacking checks; hold out one rater entirely and evaluate under CSJE to test whether Ni 2025's RLVR degradation appears on Likert SE judging and whether a distributional reward repairs it without resorting to global smoothing.
hypothesis: The hard median reward reproduces the degradation: entropy collapses, Low-stratum CRPS and held-out-rater NLL worsen while High-stratum accuracy is unchanged. The per-rater CRPS reward keeps High-stratum accuracy and raises Low-stratum CRPS and entropy-to-Low AUROC, but only under rater-level hold-out; with item-level hold-out alone it can hack the reward by uniformly inflating entropy (global smoothing, no AUROC gain), which the CSJE diagnostics expose. Mechanism: a median reward is maximised by a deterministic mode, whereas a per-rater proper score is maximised only by the true rater pmf. Either outcome is publishable: if RL with any reward degrades disagreement modelling, RL is the culprit, not the reward.
mve: benchmark: CM What/Why (800 items, 6 raters); split by diff (640/160) and by rater (reward sees raters 1-5, rater 6 unseen, rotate 3 times); CS-Java as a 3-rater stress test. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with LoRA via trl GRPO (G=8, ~1k-token prompts, 2 epochs, HF generation; 22 GB/GPU); Qwen3-14B if memory allows. Output: short CoT then a point score (R1/R2) or a 5-bin distribution (R3/R4). | objective: R1 = 1[s = pooled median]; R2 = 1[s = rating of a uniformly drawn training rater]; R3 = -CRPS(q, r_k) with r_k drawn per rollout; R4 = R3 with entropy bonus/penalty ablation. Non-RL control: SFT with KL to the pooled pmf (Chen-style) and plain median SFT. | comparison: R1 vs R2 vs R3 vs R4 vs SFT-soft vs SFT-median vs zero-shot, on the unseen rater, by stratum. | metric: Per-stratum HCA and Delta_match vs the unseen rater, CRPS and held-out-rater NLL, entropy-to-Low-stratum AUROC (smoothing-vs-disagreement test), mean predicted entropy by stratum, and reward-curve diagnostics for hacking. | est_gpu_hours: 8-12 for the full grid (4 rewards x 2 criteria x rotations); pilot R1 vs R3 on What, one rotation, about 2-3.
contribution_type: new method (per-rater proper-scoring RL reward) + empirical finding
risk: MEDIUM-HIGH (GRPO instability on 640 prompts; memory headroom on shared GPUs)
prior_work: 2506.19467: Ni et al. observe RLVR hurts disagreement modelling on NLP classification without training judges; we train the judges, on ordinal SE Likert data, and isolate reward type as the cause. ; 2510.00263: Li et al. use GRPO with Brier/log rewards on binary population preferences from synthetic personas; we use an ordinal CRPS reward against individual real raters with rater-level hold-out. ; 2505.10320: J1 manufactures verifiability for subjective prompts; we keep the subjectivity and score the distribution instead. ; 2504.00050: JudgeLRM uses hard outcome rewards vs one label; our R1 is that baseline. ; 2603.17145: REAL rewards regression/correlation to a single numeric gold; no rater pmf, no strata. ; 2507.16806: RLCR's Brier reward calibrates P(correct) for single-truth tasks; our target is P(another rater would say s). ; 2607.04332: Tan et al. warn confidence rewards are hackable; our rater-level hold-out plus entropy-AUROC diagnostic is a concrete hacking test for distributional rewards. ; 2605.20740: Park et al. use leave-one-out CRPS for LLM scalar regression; we transfer the idea to judge training over human rater panels and evaluate under CSJE. ; 2505.12301: Chen et al.'s KL SFT is our non-RL control; they evaluate on the same pooled pmf, we evaluate on an unseen rater by stratum.
so_what: Settles whether the current RL-judge recipe (RM-R1/J1/JudgeLRM-style hard rewards) is structurally incapable of representing SE disagreement, and supplies a drop-in reward that small labs can use with 3-9 rater panels.

summary: Instead of rater-ID or demographic conditioning (which memorises), condition the judge on k=8 anchor items with the target rater's own ratings, train on raters 1-4 of the 6-rater commit-message panel with anchors resampled each step, and evaluate on raters 5-6 who never appear in training, decomposing the gain into rater scale (captured by a PEBS-style affine fit on the same anchors) versus item-conditional taste; then use the anchored judge as a rater-specific selector in the offline best-of-n testbed.
hypothesis: A large share of SE Low-stratum disagreement is rater stringency (the Why floor: whether implicit rationale counts), so anchoring lifts agreement with unseen raters mostly on Low/Partial items. On What the affine baseline captures most of the gain (pure scale shift); on Why the anchored judge beats the affine baseline because floor behaviour is item-conditional (implicit-rationale items), not a global shift. Rater-ID conditioning fails on unseen raters, replicating Orlikowski in SE. Downstream, rater-specific selection beats pooled selection for that rater only on contested pools.
mve: benchmark: CM 800 items x What/Why, 6 raters (train raters 1-4, test 5-6, rotate); CoReEval readability 200 x 9 raters (train 6, test 3); CS-Java 3 raters for the BoN consequence (leave-one-rater-out anchoring). | base_model: Zero-shot pilot: Qwen3-14B with in-context anchors (no training, ~1 GPU-h). Then LoRA on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct with anchors sampled per rater per step (8 anchor items excluded from the test items of that rater). | objective: Predict the target rater's rating given item + 8 (item, rating) anchors from the same rater; CE on the anchored rater's label (or CRPS on a 5-bin output). | comparison: (i) unconditioned pooled-median judge; (ii) unconditioned leave-one-rater-out soft judge; (iii) pooled judge + PEBS-style affine fit on the same 8 anchors (scale-only baseline); (iv) rater-ID-token conditioning (Orlikowski-style); (v) anchored judge; all scored on raters absent from training. | metric: Agreement (alpha, HCA) with the unseen target rater by stratum; share of the anchored gain explained by the affine baseline; BoN: held-out-rater rating of the candidate selected for that rater vs pooled selection, contested vs uncontested pools. | est_gpu_hours: 1 (zero-shot pilot) + 3-4 (LoRA, rotations).
contribution_type: new method (few-shot rater anchoring) + empirical finding with a downstream consequence
risk: MEDIUM (6 raters means only 2 unseen raters per rotation; gains may be scale-only, which is still a clean finding)
prior_work: 2502.20897: Orlikowski show ID/demographic fine-tunes memorise annotators; we condition on the rater's own ratings (meta-learning), which generalises by construction to raters absent from training, and we include their setup as a baseline. ; 2606.27578: PEBS fits a post-hoc per-rater affine on held-out data for scalar RMs; we use it as the scale-only baseline inside a generative Likert judge and measure what remains beyond scale. ; 2408.10075: VPL infers a latent user embedding from pairwise chat preferences; ours is in-context anchoring on ordinal SE ratings with unseen-rater, stratified evaluation. ; 2406.08469: PAL learns prototype mixtures over users; no generative judge, no unseen-rater SE evaluation, no selection consequence. ; 2202.02950: Jury learning models every known annotator; our judge must handle a rater it has never seen. ; 2604.08425: DiADEM predicts who disagrees from demographics; we steer the judgment itself from rating anchors.
so_what: If a few anchor ratings from a reviewer let a judge rate like that reviewer, SE teams can personalise automated commit-message or summary review to their own standards, and the scale-vs-taste decomposition tells how much SE disagreement is merely stringency.

summary: Simulate annotation budgets on the real 3/6/9-rater SE panels: seed every item with two ratings, then spend the remaining budget uniformly, randomly, by first-two-human disagreement, by the judge's predicted spread, or by a combination, and measure how well each policy recovers the full-panel disagreement structure (Low-stratum membership, Krippendorff alpha, pooled median) and how tight the resulting HCA confidence intervals are at equal rating cost.
hypothesis: Judge-spread allocation recovers Low-stratum membership with roughly 30% fewer ratings than uniform; the honest human-only baseline (first-two-rater disagreement) is strong, but judge spread adds most where the first two raters agree by chance (e.g. the Why-floor items where 13% of ratings are non-zero), so the combined policy dominates; full-panel alpha is recoverable with about 60% of the ratings. Mechanism: the judge's score-token spread is a cheap per-item prior on dispersion that two ratings cannot reveal. A null result (judge spread ~ random) is itself a finding: judge uncertainty is not a per-item disagreement signal in SE.
mve: benchmark: CM 800 items x What/Why (6 raters), CS-Java (3 raters, sanity), CoReEval readability 200 x 9 raters; budgets B = 0.5x, 1x, 2x the item count in extra ratings. | base_model: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct zero-shot score-token distributions (10 min) and the 3-run frontier outputs as spread proxies; optionally the TS4/TS5 trained distributional judge. | objective: Allocation policies: uniform; random; human-disagreement-first (|r1-r2|); judge-spread-first (predicted entropy/variance); combined (judge spread where r1=r2, human disagreement otherwise); oracle (true full-panel range). | comparison: Policies at equal budget, 200 simulation seeds, all three panels. | metric: F1 for recovering full-panel Low-stratum labels; MAE of pooled median; absolute error of Krippendorff alpha; bootstrap CI width of a fixed judge's HCA estimated from the subsampled panel; ratings needed to reach 90% of full-panel stratum recovery. | est_gpu_hours: <=0.5.
contribution_type: protocol + empirical finding
prior_work: 2602.02550: HyPAC replaces human annotations against one gold label; our estimand is the disagreement structure itself (strata, alpha, HCA CI), which pooled-label methods cannot target. ; 2403.07008: PPI-style AutoEval estimates pooled quantities from few humans plus judge outputs; we allocate human ratings rather than substitute them, and target dispersion. ; 2408.15204: Confidence-driven inference uses LLM confidence to pick which items humans label, for classification accuracy vs gold; we target rater dispersion on ordinal SE ratings. ; 2410.13341: Dorner et al. bound the value of judge outputs as extra data for a pooled estimand; allocation of human ratings is outside that bound. ; 2310.15638: CoAnnotating allocates items between humans and LLMs by uncertainty against gold; we allocate additional raters per item and include the human-disagreement baseline they omit. ; 2605.01168: Zhang and Coltekin predict rating variance from text on NLP data; we use the judge's spread operationally to build panels and validate on SE. ; 2503.03064: Wang et al. show judgment distributions predict pairwise disagreement at inference; we turn that into a collection policy and evaluate recovery of strata.
so_what: Gives benchmark builders a concrete recipe for the paper's own recommendation to 'release annotator-level ratings': how many raters each item needs and how a cheap judge can direct that spend toward the items whose disagreement the benchmark must capture.

summary: Test the default judge-training assumption that the pooled median is the right SFT target: does SFT-to-median make a 7B SE judge track the panel median more tightly than a matched held-out human on contested items, i.e. does pooled-label training manufacture the alignment mirage inside the model rather than only in the measurement?
hypothesis: Pooled-median SFT collapses the score-token distribution toward the denoised median. On Low-consensus items, agreement with the pooled median rises (the standard score improves) while agreement with a held-out rater does not, so Delta_match widens after training; entropy-to-Low AUROC falls because the judge becomes confidently central; the High-stratum shortfall shrinks only modestly. Mechanism: the median has lower variance than any single rater, so CE-to-median rewards exactly the behaviour CSJE flags. A rater-sampled hard-label target (each item replicated once per rater, same mean, dispersion preserved) should widen Delta_match less. Publishable either way: 'training amplifies the mirage' or 'the mirage is purely a measurement artifact that training leaves untouched' (a training-side confirmation of the paper's F2/F3).
mve: Benchmark: commit messages (800 items x 6 raters, What and Why). Base: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, LoRA r=16, ~1k tokens/item, 3 epochs, 5-fold item CV so every item is scored unseen. Arms: A0 base (no training); A1 SFT to pooled median; A2 SFT to rater-sampled labels (item x 6 replicas, one per rater); A3 SFT to rounded mean (sanity). Judge output = argmax and expected value of the 0-4 score-token pmf, fed to idea-stage/pilot/csje_eval.py full_report. Metrics per stratum: alpha_HL vs pooled median, alpha_ref, Delta_match, HCA with bootstrap CI, a median-tracking index MTI = alpha(judge, median) - alpha(judge, held-out rater) averaged over held-out choices, entropy-to-Low AUROC, held-out-rater NLL. Comparison: A1 vs A0 vs A2 reported under pooled-only and under CSJE. Cost: ~0.3 GPU-h per LoRA run, 3 arms x 5 folds ~ 5 GPU-h; single-fold pilot ~ 1.5 GPU-h on one RTX 6000 Ada.
contribution_type: empirical finding + protocol (training-time mirage audit)
prior_work: Chen 2025 (2505.12301) compares point-SFT with KL-to-pooled-pmf on the same pooled target and never asks whether point-SFT changes agreement with a held-out rater by stratum. Huang 2024 (2403.02839) shows fine-tuned judges become task classifiers, but against single labels. Zhang 2025 (2410.14632) finds BT RMs equally decisive on diverging and consensual pairs, but does not train on pooled vs disaggregated targets or score against a matched human. Xiao 2024 (2405.16455) and Slocum 2025 (2511.08594) predict majority amplification for policies in theory/synthetic groups; never measured for a trained judge on a real small panel. Delta: first measurement of what the pooled target does to a judge relative to a held-out human, by consensus stratum, on real SE ratings.
so_what: If pooled SFT widens Delta_match, every distilled SE judge and every RM trained on CodeUltraFeedback-style pooled scores is optimising toward the artifact CSJE exposes, and 'tune to the aggregate-best score' becomes a documented harm with a cheap fix (rater-sampled targets). If it does not, the paper's 'mirage is measurement, not model' claim gains training-side evidence.

summary: Test the assumption that a judge's per-item uncertainty (token entropy, run-to-run sampling variance, verbalized confidence) encodes item-level human disagreement, against the null that it is a global temperature plus a scale-location effect (the Why floor / ceiling), using location-controlled disagreement metrics on held-out raters.
hypothesis: Most of the apparent entropy-to-Low AUROC is explained by location: a 0-4 pmf near the floor is mechanically peaked and the Why criterion has a heavy zero floor, so entropy separates floor-vs-mid-scale rather than agreed-vs-contested (the smoke test already shows base Qwen peaking at 2-3 on items where all six humans give Why=0). Conditioning on the judge's own predicted level, or fitting a location-only dispersion model P(rating | predicted level), will absorb most of the signal; sampling variance across the three frontier runs will be near-zero and uninformative; verbalized confidence will be the weakest and largely a function of predicted level. A Chen-style KL LoRA will improve global NLL but not the location-controlled AUROC, which makes the 'smoothing vs disagreement' ambiguity (landscape gap 1) directly testable. Publishable either way: if any signal survives the control, it is the first validated item-level disagreement signal on held-out raters in SE.
mve: Benchmarks: commit messages (What, Why; Why is the floor stress test) and code summarization (3 criteria, 1-5). Signals: S1 score-token entropy and variance from Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and Qwen3-14B (inference, ~10-20 min each); S2 run-to-run variance of the existing Claude Opus 4.8 / Gemini 3.1 Pro / GPT-5.5 triplicate runs (free); S3 verbalized confidence, one extra OpenRouter pass with a 'probability another expert rater gives the same score' prompt on 800 CM items (~5-10 USD); S4 Chen-style KL-to-pooled-pmf LoRA on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, 5-fold (~2 GPU-h). Null models: N1 global temperature + per-level bias fit on training folds; N2 location-only dispersion, the empirical human pmf conditional on the judge's predicted level. Metrics: held-out-rater NLL and CRPS (csje_eval.heldout_nll / crps) for each signal vs N1/N2; entropy-to-Low AUROC raw and location-controlled (AUROC within bins of predicted level, weighted, or partial AUROC after regressing out predicted level); per-stratum dispersion calibration with split-panel realization (dispersion among raters 4-6 given a predictor fit on raters 1-3). Cost ~2.5 GPU-h plus a small API spend.
contribution_type: diagnostic / protocol (location-controlled disagreement metric) + empirical finding
prior_work: Wang/Zhang/Choi 2025 (2503.03064) show token distributions predict pairwise disagreement without controlling for scale location. Zhang 2025 (2410.14632) Diverging-ID AUROC is likewise uncontrolled and has no held-out rater. Chen 2025 (2505.12301) and Li 2025 (2510.00263) report KL/Brier to the same pooled distribution, so global smoothing and item-level information are indistinguishable. Tian 2025 (2508.06225) documents judge over-confidence against one gold label. Baan 2022 (2210.16133) argues for instance-level calibration under disagreement without a location control. Nine Judges (2605.29800) and Judge-Knows (2608.07517) score vote margins against majority labels. Inoshita 2026 (2604.27345) finds LLMs match labels but not uncertainty, on emotion NLP. Delta: three uncertainty families compared head-to-head against a location-only null and against held-out raters, on ordinal SE panels with a floor effect.
so_what: Every uncertainty-based routing scheme (Trust-or-Escalate 2407.18370, HyPAC 2602.02550, SCOPE 2602.13110, Gupta 2604.15302) assumes the judge's uncertainty is item-level; if it is location-driven, escalation forwards floor/ceiling items instead of contested ones. The output is a named, releasable protocol (location-controlled disagreement AUROC / calibration) that any disagreement-aware judge paper should report.

summary: Test whether a 3-9-rater panel is enough to define a distributional training target: for each panel size k, measure how well the k-rater empirical pmf (and shrunk or pooled alternatives) predicts a held-out rater, and whether a judge trained on that target inherits the ordering, giving a sample-size curve for the training target itself.
hypothesis: Below a crossover k* (expected around 4-5 on the 0-4 CM scale, higher on the low-power readability panel), the raw k-rater empirical pmf is a worse predictor of a held-out rater than a shrunk target (Dirichlet smoothing toward a global or stratum-level dispersion, or median + ordinal kernel), because with few raters the empirical pmf is dominated by sampling spikes. A judge trained with KL to the raw pmf learns those spikes rather than disagreement structure, and trained judges inherit the target ordering, so the optimal distributional target for small panels is shrunk, not the empirical pmf used by Chen 2025 / Singh 2025. The oracle k-rater target's held-out-rater NLL also gives a 'target noise floor' that upper-bounds any judge trained on k raters, a number no distributional-judge paper reports.
mve: Stage 1 (CPU, hours): for CM (m=6), readability (m=9) and CS (m=3), enumerate rater subsets of size k=1..m-1; targets: raw empirical pmf, Dirichlet(alpha) smoothing toward uniform, smoothing toward stratum-level dispersion, pooled median as one-hot, median + global ordinal dispersion kernel; score each on the held-out raters with csje_eval.heldout_nll and crps; report the crossover k* per benchmark and criterion. Stage 2 (GPU): Qwen2.5-Coder-7B LoRA with KL-to-target on CM, k in {2,3,5} x 2 random subsets, raw vs best shrunk target; evaluate on held-out raters and on CSJE Delta_match and HCA. ~12 runs x 0.3 GPU-h ~ 4 GPU-h; pilot with k in {2,5}, raw vs shrunk ~ 1.2 GPU-h.
contribution_type: empirical finding + protocol (target noise floor, sample-size curve) + light method (shrunk ordinal target)
prior_work: Chen 2025 (2505.12301) trains on the raw empirical pmf with an ad-hoc adversarial l2 ball and never reports what panel size supports the target. Singh 2025 (2511.14117) and LeWiDi-2025 (2510.08460) take the soft label as given. Fang 2026 (2605.11865) flags mean+variance identifiability from few raters as open, in the pairwise RM setting. PEBS (2606.27578) needs per-rater held-out data and does per-rater affine calibration, not target shrinkage. Artificial Hivemind (2510.22954) works at 25 ratings/item and never studies the small-panel regime. Delta: first rater-count curve for the distributional target, with a held-out-rater noise floor and a training-side confirmation.
so_what: Tells SE benchmark builders how many raters to collect before releasing a distributional target and tells judge trainers that Chen-style losses should use a shrunk target at 3-6 raters; it turns the paper's 'release annotator-level ratings' implication into a quantitative requirement.

summary: Test whether a judge trained on LLM-generated artifacts (the norm for SE judge and RM training data) transfers to human-authored artifacts, using the commit-message benchmark's 400 developer-written vs 400 generated messages rated by the same six developers. (Note: the CM 'pools' are artifact populations, not rater populations; rater-population transfer is not testable within one fixed panel here.)
hypothesis: The two pools have different consensus landscapes: generated messages carry a Why floor, while roughly half the developer-pool Why items are Low-consensus. A judge LoRA-trained on generated-pool labels learns a floor-dominated Why scale and transfers poorly to developer messages, with the loss concentrated in the Low stratum and hidden under pooled alpha because floor items dominate agreement; the reverse direction transfers better. The cross-pool gap will exceed the within-pool item-split generalization gap, i.e. artifact authorship is the dominant shift, and it will be invisible in pooled scoring but large in Delta_match.
mve: CM benchmark; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B LoRA to pooled median (and a rater-sampled variant). Arms: train generated -> test developer; train developer -> test generated; within-pool 5-fold for each pool as reference. Metrics: per-stratum alpha_HL, alpha_ref, Delta_match, HCA, held-out-rater NLL; pmf-shape diagnostics (judge mass at Why=0 vs human mass at 0). ~14 runs x 0.3 GPU-h ~ 4 GPU-h; two cross-pool arms as pilot ~ 0.7 GPU-h.
contribution_type: empirical finding (SE-specific distribution-shift result)
prior_work: Zeng 2025 (2507.10906) averages raters and scores both pools with pooled metrics. CodeUltraFeedback (2403.09032), CodeFavor (2410.03837) and BigCodeArena (2510.08697) train or benchmark on LLM outputs only. Huang 2024 (2403.02839) reports weak cross-task generalization of fine-tuned judges, not cross-authorship. Mokhova 2026 (2605.25296) shows LLM Likert distributions polarize relative to engineers but trains nothing. Delta: first authorship-transfer test of a trained SE judge with a matched-human, stratified readout.
so_what: SE judges are trained on model outputs but deployed on human code (review bots, commit-lint, PR triage). If transfer failure concentrates on contested human-authored items and is invisible to pooled scoring, that is a concrete benchmark-construction rule (stratify by authorship and consensus) and a warning about CodeUltraFeedback-style training sets.

summary: Test whether item-disjoint splits suffice to validate a distributional judge: train on raters 1..k's pmf and evaluate against never-seen raters (rater-disjoint split) to measure how much of the reported distributional gain is panel-specific.
hypothesis: A distributional judge trained with KL/CRPS to the full panel's pmf gets part of its item-split gain from panel idiosyncrasies (the specific six developers' scale use, e.g. one rater's strictness on Why, visible in Zeng's volunteer correlation matrix), not from item-level disagreement. Under a rater-disjoint split (train on the pmf of raters {1..4}, test NLL/CRPS on raters {5,6}, all 15 such splits) the gain over pooled-median SFT shrinks substantially, and the judge's predicted pmf is closer to the training raters' pmf than to the held-out raters' pmf by more than the human-human rater-split gap. If the gain survives, that is the first non-circular validation of a distributional judge. The readability panel (9 raters, S=0.14) gives a second, noisier replication.
mve: CM: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B LoRA with KL to the training-rater pmf (Chen-style without the adversarial term) vs CE to the training-rater median, under three split regimes: item-only (raters shared), rater-only (items shared, raters disjoint), both disjoint. Metrics: NLL/CRPS vs held-out raters; a panel-specificity index = KL(q || p_train-raters) - KL(q || p_held-out-raters) compared with the human baseline KL(p_train || p_held-out); CSJE per stratum on the held-out raters. 2 losses x 5 sampled rater splits x 2 item folds ~ 20 runs x 0.3 GPU-h ~ 6 GPU-h; pilot 2 losses x 1 rater split ~ 0.7 GPU-h. Readability replication: same with 5-vs-4 rater splits, ~2 GPU-h.
contribution_type: protocol (rater-disjoint validation) + empirical finding
prior_work: Orlikowski 2025 (2502.20897) shows per-annotator fine-tuning memorises annotators, on NLP perception tasks, for annotator-conditioned models, without a judge task. Chen 2025 (2505.12301) and Li 2025 (2510.00263) use item splits with the same raters on both sides. PEBS (2606.27578) holds out ratings per rater for calibration, not for validating a trained judge. Guerdan 2025 (2503.05965) argues for validation under indeterminacy but without rater-disjoint splits. Delta: rater-disjoint evaluation of a distributional (not annotator-conditioned) judge, with a panel-specificity index benchmarked against the human rater-split gap.
so_what: Settles whether 'learned the disagreement structure' claims survive an unseen panel, the same evaluation-contract question the paper raised for pooled labels, now at training time; ships a reusable split protocol for the three released SE panels.

summary: Test whether human disagreement on SE artifacts is predictable from artifact features (hence learnable) rather than rater noise, using split-panel validation: predict one half-panel's dispersion from features and check it against the other half-panel's dispersion.
hypothesis: SE disagreement is partly structured around known trade-offs: in code summarization, the conciseness-vs-content-adequacy tension (short summaries split raters on CA but not on conciseness; cross-criterion splits within an item are themselves a feature); in commit messages, rationale cues and diff size drive Why disagreement; in readability, disagreement is unstructured (S=0.14, noise-dominated). Expected feature-based Low-stratum AUROC ~0.65-0.75 on CS/CM and ~0.5 on readability, with split-panel replication separating structured disagreement from panel noise. A 7B judge's token entropy will underperform the feature model, and a 7B LoRA trained to predict dispersion directly will match the feature model only on the structured benchmarks.
mve: CPU stage: features (summary and code token lengths and ratios, diff line counts, rationale cue words such as because / so that / fix, cross-criterion disagreement, base-model perplexity of the artifact) -> logistic / GBM predicting Low stratum and rater std under item CV; split-panel validation on CM (3 vs 3 raters) and readability (4 vs 5); on CS (3 raters) leave-one-rater-out dispersion. GPU stage: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B dispersion-regression LoRA (target: std of training raters), 5-fold, ~1.5 GPU-h; compare to token entropy. Metrics: AUROC for Low on held-out half-panel, Spearman with held-out-half dispersion, and a learnability ceiling = AUROC of one half-panel's dispersion predicting the other half's (the human noise ceiling).
contribution_type: empirical finding + diagnostic (per-benchmark disagreement learnability ceiling)
prior_work: Zhang and Coltekin 2026 (2605.01168) predict rating variance from text in NLP without split-panel validation or trade-off features. DiADEM (2604.08425) predicts who disagrees from demographics. Zhang 2025 (2410.14632) gives a taxonomy of diverging-preference causes on chat data and an RM-based Diverging-ID AUROC, not artifact features and not held-out raters. Ehara 2026 (2605.12422) predicts judge-human disagreement for CEFR. Crupi 2025 (2507.16587) releases three-criterion ratings but never analyses cross-criterion disagreement. Delta: split-panel learnability ceiling plus SE trade-off features, across three panels.
so_what: Supplies the missing premise for any disagreement-aware SE judge: the learnability ceiling says whether a judge can be trained to flag contested items at all on a given benchmark, and the trade-off features give concrete content to the paper's 'escalate contested items' implication (what makes an SE item contested).
